title: A report query takes 30 seconds on every request — how do you fix it?
description: From index triage to pre-aggregated summary tables, incremental rollups, and staleness trade-offs.

data.text: A 30-second report usually means the same expensive aggregate — GROUP BY over millions of rows with joins — is being recomputed on every request. Fixing it is a ladder: confirm the plan and statistics (index coverage, misestimates, missing indexes), remove accidental full scans (functions on columns, implicit conversions, client-side evaluation), and if the query is inherently O(table), stop recomputing it: pre-aggregate into summary tables, indexes, or materialized views and refresh them incrementally.

The interviewer is testing whether you move from 'tune the query' to 'change the computation strategy' — and whether you're honest about the new trade-off: pre-aggregation trades write complexity and staleness for constant-time reads. Candidates who only know 'add an index' stall here; candidates who can discuss refresh cadence, backfill, and consistency windows sound like they've shipped this.
Step 1: verify what the 30 seconds is spent on

items: Read the actual plan: look for high-cost scans, key lookups per row, sorts spilling to tempdb, and estimate-vs-actual cardinality gaps (stale statistics or parameter sniffing).
Check for accidental non-sargable predicates: WHERE CONVERT(date, CreatedAt) = @d or LIKE '%term%' or implicit conversion from nvarchar parameter to varchar column — each forces scans.
Check row volume versus semantics: does the report need every row, or aggregates that only change hourly?
Measure separately: engine time vs network (SELECT * of wide aggregates), serialization, and ORM overhead (materializing 500k entities to count them in memory).
Rule out the usual suspects first: missing index for the GROUP BY/JOIN keys, top-N operators pulling 20 rows from a 10M-row sort each request.

data.text: Step 2: change the computation — summary tables

data.title: Pre-aggregated daily summary, refreshed incrementally
data.code:
-- The report: 30s over raw events every request
SELECT CAST(OrderedAt AS date) AS Day, Region, COUNT(*) AS Orders, SUM(Total) AS Revenue
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderedAt >= DATEADD(day, -90, GETUTCDATE())
GROUP BY CAST(OrderedAt AS date), Region;

-- The fix: maintain the aggregate once, read it in milliseconds
CREATE TABLE OrderDailySummary (
    Day         date        NOT NULL,
    Region      varchar(10) NOT NULL,
    Orders      int         NOT NULL,
    Revenue     decimal(18,2) NOT NULL,
    UpdatedAt   datetime2   NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (Day, Region)
);

-- Full build (once, at migration time)
INSERT INTO OrderDailySummary (Day, Region, Orders, Revenue, UpdatedAt)
SELECT CAST(OrderedAt AS date), Region, COUNT(*), SUM(Total), SYSUTCDATETIME()
FROM Orders GROUP BY CAST(OrderedAt AS date), Region;

-- Incremental refresh: only today's partition (runs every minute as a job)
MERGE OrderDailySummary AS t
USING (
    SELECT CAST(OrderedAt AS date) AS Day, Region, COUNT(*) AS Orders, SUM(Total) AS Revenue
    FROM Orders
    WHERE OrderedAt >= CAST(GETUTCDATE() AS date)     -- touched range only
    GROUP BY CAST(OrderedAt AS date), Region
) AS s ON t.Day = s.Day AND t.Region = s.Region
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.Orders = s.Orders, t.Revenue = s.Revenue,
                             t.UpdatedAt = SYSUTCDATETIME()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (Day, Region, Orders, Revenue, UpdatedAt)
                      VALUES (s.Day, s.Region, s.Orders, s.Revenue, SYSUTCDATETIME());

-- Read path for the report: index scan of a few hundred rows
SELECT * FROM OrderDailySummary WHERE Day BETWEEN @from AND @to ORDER BY Day;

items: Scheduled rollup (above): simplest; staleness = refresh interval; ideal for dashboards that tolerate minutes.

Incremental on write: trigger from the app after committing a sale (append to today's row) — near-real-time, but doubles write-path work and needs care under concurrency (atomic UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1 or a queue).
Event-driven rebuild: consume the outbox stream and update summaries per event — real-time, builds on the messaging machinery you already have.
Late-arriving data: refunds and backfills touch old days — keep a reconciliation job that rebuilds the affected window overnight.

Database-native options: indexed views (SQL Server: schema-bound, restrictive but zero ETL) and materialized views (PostgreSQL: CONCURRENTLY refresh without blocking reads) trade flexibility for engine-managed maintenance.
The honest staleness statement: label reports 'as of 2 minutes ago' and make sure product/finance agree with the window.

data.title: Pre-aggregation is a consistency trade, not a free lunch
data.text: Summary tables answer from yesterday's math: every read becomes cheap, every write becomes slightly heavier, and a broken refresh job turns into a silent wrong-number incident. Alert on summary lag (MAX(UpdatedAt) vs now) the same way you'd alert on queue depth — otherwise staleness fails invisibly.

A strong answer walks the ladder: (1) is the plan bad — fix statistics, sargability, indexes; (2) is the query O(table) by nature — pre-aggregate; (3) what's the staleness budget and who signed off on it; (4) how do we backfill, reconcile late data, and alert when refresh lags. You also mention what you will NOT do: cache the 30-second query with a long TTL (masks the problem, freezes wrongness), or let users export full-table scans into your primary database — reporting workloads belong on replicas or pre-aggregated storage so analytical reads can't starve transactional ones.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: First prove the plan: scans, non-sargable predicates, estimate gaps, spills.
Inherently O(table) reports should not run per request — pre-aggregate.
Refresh incrementally (partition window or events) and reconcile late data.
Declare staleness explicitly and alert on summary lag.
Heavy analytics belong on replicas/summary storage, not the OLTP primary.
data.takeaway: Stop recomputing what changes slowly: fix the plan, then move the math to write time and read the pre-aggregated result — with lag measured and alerted.
